source_evidence.full_current_interface: Let $v_0,\ldots,v_{m-1}\in\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q$, $m\ge3$, be the cyclically ordered vertices of a simple strictly convex polygon whose edges are traversed counterclockwise. Let $P$ be its filled convex hull and let $\Gamma$ be the concatenation of its oriented edges. For every $z\notin\Gamma$, the winding number $n(\Gamma,z)$ is $1$ if $z\in\operatorname{int}P$ and $0$ if $z\notin P$.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f$ be an autonomous $C^1$ vector field, let $\gamma(t)=\phi_t(x_*)$ be a nonconstant periodic solution of period $T>0$, and let $M=D_x\phi_T(x_*)$ be its monodromy matrix. Then
$$
M f(x_*)=f(x_*).
$$
In particular, $1$ is a Floquet multiplier.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Time translation along a nonconstant autonomous periodic orbit gives a nonzero tangent eigenvector of monodromy with multiplier one.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Nonconstancy implies $f(x_*)\ne0$: otherwise the constant curve through $x_*$ is an IVP solution, and uniqueness in [F2] forces $\gamma$ to be that constant curve. [given, F2]

2.1 Differentiate the flow identity in [F2] with respect to $s$ at $s=0$. The chain rule [F3] gives $D_x\phi_T(x_*)f(x_*)$ on the left, while the time derivative on the right is $f(\phi_T(x_*))=f(x_*)$. By [F1] the left derivative is the monodromy action, hence $Mf(x_*)=f(x_*)$. Since $f(x_*)\ne0$ by step 1.1, this is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $1$, which is a Floquet multiplier by [F4]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ on an open set $U$. Let $T_+>0$, let $W\subset U$ be open, and suppose every solution from $x\in W$ exists on an open time interval containing $[0,T_+]$ and stays in one compact convex set $K\subset U$ for all $t\in[0,T_+]$. Write $\Phi(t,x)=\phi_t(x)$. Then $\Phi$ is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,x)$ on $(0,T_+)\times W$, locally on every common-tube neighborhood in $W$, and its derivatives extend continuously in time to $[0,T_+]$. Its first state derivative $S(t,x)=D_x\Phi(t,x)$ solves
$$
\partial_t S=Df(\Phi)S,\qquad S(0,x)=I_n,
$$
and its second state derivative is the bilinear map $H(t,x)$ determined by
$$
\partial_t H[u,v]=Df(\Phi)H[u,v]+D^2f(\Phi)[S u,S v],\qquad H(0,x)[u,v]=0.
$$
In particular $\partial_t\Phi=f(\Phi)$, $\partial_{tx}\Phi=Df(\Phi)S$, and $\partial_{tt}\Phi=Df(\Phi)f(\Phi)$. The assertion is local to the stated common tube.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A common compact convex trajectory tube supplies joint flow derivatives, first and second variational equations and continuous time-endpoint extensions.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Fix a base state $x\in W$. By [F1], $\Phi$ is $C^1$ in $x$ and $S$ solves $S'=A S$, where $A(t)=Df(\Phi(t,x))$. The coefficient is bounded on $[0,T_+]$ by [F3]; integrating the variational equation by [F6] and applying [F5] bounds $S$ uniformly in $t$. The flow itself is jointly continuous in $(t,x)$ on the common tube by [F1] and the ODE relation [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, given]

2.2 For small $h$ with $x+h\in W$, put $\Delta(t)=\Phi(t,x+h)-\Phi(t,x)$, $S_h(t)=S(t,x+h)$, and $A_h(t)=Df(\Phi(t,x+h))$. The uniform remainder in [F1] gives $\Delta=S h+o(\|h\|_2)$ uniformly on $J$. On each segment between $\Phi(t,x)$ and $\Phi(t,x+h)$, the chain rule [F7] and [F6] applied coordinatewise to $Df$ give $ A_h-A=\int_0^1 D^2f(\Phi+s\Delta)[\Delta,\cdot] ds. $ Uniform continuity of $D^2f$ on $K$ [F3] and $\Delta=S h+o(\|h\|)$ therefore imply $A_h-A=D^2f(\Phi)[S h,\cdot]+o(\|h\|_2)$ uniformly in $t$. [F1, F3, F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface: Let $H$, $K$, the range provider, $L,M$, and the initial box $Y_0=X_0\times\{I_d\}\times\Theta$ satisfy [[def-verified-flow-variational-range-oracle]] and [[alg-validated-euler-flow-and-monodromy-enclosure]]. If that procedure returns success with boxes $Q_0,\ldots,Q_{N-1}$ and $Y_N$, then for every $(x_0,\theta)\in X_0\times\Theta$ the unique solution of $y'=H(y)$ from $(x_0,I_d,\theta)$ exists through time $1$, its trajectory on $[n/N,(n+1)/N]$ lies in $Q_n$, and its terminal state lies in $Y_N$. Consequently the endpoint state encloses $\phi_\theta(x_0)$ and the matrix block encloses $D_x\phi_\theta(x_0)$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A successful verified range-provider Euler enclosure contains every admitted scaled trajectory and terminal monodromy block through the unit interval.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Fix any exact state $y_n\in Y_n$ at time $nh$. While its solution remains in $K$, [F1] gives $\|H(y(t))\|_\infty\le M$, hence $\|y(t)-y_n\|_\infty\le M(t-nh)\le Mh$. If it first left $K$ before $nh+h$, continuity would place the exit point in $Q_n\subseteq K$, a contradiction. Thus the solution exists throughout this cell and stays in $Q_n$. [F1, F2, F3, given]

4.1 For $H(x,Z,\theta)=(\theta f(x),\theta Df(x)Z,0)$, the state block solves $x'=\theta f(x)$ and the matrix block solves $Z'=\theta Df(x)Z$ with $Z(0)=I_d$. Rescaling physical time $t=\theta s$ makes the state block $\phi_{\theta s}(x_0)$; [F4] identifies $Z(s)$ with its derivative in $x_0$. The terminal block inclusions from step 3.1 are therefore the claimed flow and monodromy enclosures. [F2, F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface: Let $\gamma$ be a nonconstant periodic orbit of least period $T$, let $x_*=\gamma(0)$, and let $M=D_x\phi_T(x_*)$. Suppose the phase multiplier $1$ is algebraically simple and $\psi(x_*)=0$ with $c^\top f(x_*)\ne0$, where $c=D\psi(x_*)$. Then the eigenvalues of the derivative of the local Poincare return map on the section $\Sigma=\{x:\psi(x)=0\}$, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are exactly the Floquet multipliers of $M$ other than the single phase multiplier $1$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A simple phase multiplier and transverse section identify the return-map spectrum with all monodromy multipliers except the single neutral phase mode.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Define $\Psi(t,x)=\psi(\phi_t(x))$. At $(T,x_*)$, $\Psi(T,x_*)=0$ and $\partial_t\Psi(T,x_*)=c^\top f(x_*)\ne0$. By [F4], there is a local return-time function $\tau(x)$ on the section with $\tau(x_*)=T$ and $\Psi(\tau(x),x)=0$. Differentiating this identity at $x_*$ in a tangent direction $v\in S:=\ker c^\top$ gives $D\tau(x_*)v=-c^\top Mv/(c^\top f(x_*))$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, given, construct]

2.1 The local return map is $P(x)=\phi_{\tau(x)}(x)$. The chain rule and step 1.1 give, for $v\in S$, $ DP(x_*)v=Mv-\frac{f(x_*)c^\top Mv}{c^\top f(x_*)}=\Pi Mv,\qquad \Pi=I-\frac{f(x_*)c^\top}{c^\top f(x_*)}. $ The map $\Pi$ identifies the quotient $\mathbb C^d/\operatorname{span}\{f(x_*)\}$ with $S$: it kills the phase direction and is the identity on $S$. Since $M f(x_*)=f(x_*)$ by [F3], it induces a linear map on this quotient, and $DP(x_*)$ is its conjugate under that identification. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, given, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $u_*(s)=(\gamma(Ts),T)$, $0\le s\le1$, be the augmented solution from [[def-phase-bordered-periodic-orbit-bvp]] for a nonconstant $C^2$ autonomous periodic orbit of period $T>0$. Assume its phase multiplier $1$ is algebraically simple and its affine phase covector $c$ satisfies $c^\top f(\gamma(0))\ne0$. For the continuous linearized BVP operator $\mathcal L:X\to Z$ of [[def-linearized-two-point-bvp-operator-and-conditioning]], define
$$ A(s)=D\widetilde f(u_*(s)),\quad a_0=\sup_{0\le s\le1}\|A(s)\|_2, \quad B_2=D_2B(u_*(0),u_*(1)),\quad K_J\ge\|J^{-1}\|_{2\to2}, $$
where $J=\begin{bmatrix}M-I&f(\gamma(0))\\c^\top&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $M=D\phi_T(\gamma(0))$. Put $E=e^{a_0}$ and
$$ K_{\mathcal L}:=(1+a_0)\left[E K_J(1+\|B_2\|_2E)+E\right]+1. $$
Then $\mathcal L$ is bijective and $\|\mathcal L^{-1}\|_{Z\to X}\le K_{\mathcal L}$, with the spaces and norms defined in [[def-linearized-two-point-bvp-operator-and-conditioning]]. All constants are finite and explicit once the stated coefficient and shooting-inverse bounds are supplied.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A simple phase multiplier and transverse phase give an explicit finite inverse norm for the continuous periodic BVP linearization in its stated norms.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 The homogeneous solution with initial value $\xi$ is $U(t,0)\xi$. Its endpoint variation is the derivative of the augmented flow. The first $d$ endpoint coordinates differentiate to $Mv+f(\gamma(0))\tau$ in initial variation $(v,\tau)$: the $v$ column is monodromy, and the period column is $\partial_T\phi_T(\gamma(0))=f(\gamma(0))$ by [F5] and periodicity. Differentiating $B(u_0,u_1)=(x_1-x_0,\psi(x_0))$ by [F7] therefore gives $B_1+B_2U(1,0)=J$. [F1, F2, F5, F7, step 1.1]

2.2 For data $(g,q)\in Z$, let $p$ be the unique solution of $p'=Ap+g$, $p(0)=0$. Local existence and uniqueness follow from [F3]; integrating this equation by [F6] gives $\|p(t)\|_2\le\|g\|_\infty+a_0\int_0^t\|p(s)\|_2ds$, hence $\|p\|_\infty\le E\|g\|_\infty$ by [F4]. This bound extends $p$ through the full interval by [F3]. Every solution with initial value $\xi$ equals $U(t,0)\xi+p(t)$, since their difference solves the homogeneous linear IVP with initial value $\xi$ and uniqueness [F3] applies. [F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Consider the augmented phase-fixed BVP of [[def-phase-bordered-periodic-orbit-bvp]] on $[0,1]$, with exact solution $u_*\in C^3$, field $\widetilde f$, and affine boundary map $B$. Put
$$M_2=\|u_*''\|_\infty,\quad M_3=\|u_*'''\|_\infty,\quad L_f=\sup\|D\widetilde f\|_2,\quad C_0=M_3/24+L_fM_2/8.$$
For every admitted mesh cell with midpoint $m_i$, assume the segment joining $u_*(m_i)$ to $(u_*(t_i)+u_*(t_{i+1}))/2$ lies in the field domain and $\|D\widetilde f\|_{\rm op}\le L_f$ on that segment. Let $G_h$ be the normalized midpoint residual on a uniform mesh and $Y^*$ the samples of $u_*$. Suppose that for all $0<h\le h_0$, $J_h=DG_h(Y^*)$ is invertible with $\|J_h^{-1}\|_{\infty\to\infty}\le K$, and on a fixed-radius ball of radius $r$ about $Y^*$ the maps $DG_h$ are $L_G$-Lipschitz in the block maximum norm. Assume $2KL_Gr\le1/2$, $KC_0h^2\le r/2$, and $2K^2L_GC_0h^2\le1/2$. Then $G_h$ has a unique zero $Y_h$ in that ball. Every candidate $Y$ in the ball satisfying $\|G_h(Y)\|_\infty\le\varepsilon$ obeys
$$
\|P_hY-u_*\|_\infty\le 4K\varepsilon+\left(2KC_0+\frac{M_2}{8}\right)h^2,
$$
where $P_h$ is linear interpolation of the node values. Thus the residual and discretization constants are explicit in the supplied derivative and inverse bounds. For the augmented state, the estimate includes both the orbit coordinates and the period coordinate.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Uniform residual-Jacobian inverse and Lipschitz bounds yield a unique nearby collocation zero plus explicit residual and quadratic-mesh interpolation error for orbit and period.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 On a mesh cell centered at $m_i$, repeated vector FTC gives $u_*'(m_i+s)=u_*'(m_i)+s u_*''(m_i)+r(s)$, where $r(s)=\int_0^s\int_0^v u_*'''(m_i+w)\,dw\,dv$. For negative limits reverse their orientation before applying the norm inequality. Thus $\|r(s)\|_2\le M_3|s|^2/2$. Averaging over $[-h/2,h/2]$ cancels the odd term and gives a difference-quotient defect at most $M_3h^2/24$. Applying the same integral argument to $u_*$ at $m_i\pm h/2$ bounds each first-order remainder by $M_2h^2/8$; their average therefore bounds the endpoint-average displacement from $u_*(m_i)$ by $M_2h^2/8$. Integrating $D\widetilde f$ on the connecting segment bounds the corresponding field difference by $L_fM_2h^2/8$. The affine boundary residual is zero. Taking the maximum of the cell bounds gives $\|G_h(Y^*)\|_\infty\le C_0h^2$. [F1, F4, F6, F7, given, algebra]

3.1 The perturbation bound $\|DG_h(Y_h)-J_h\|\le L_G\|Y_h-Y^*\|$ implies $\|J_h^{-1}(DG_h(Y_h)-J_h)\|\le2K^2L_GC_0h^2\le1/2$. The small-perturbation inverse bound [F5] therefore gives $DG_h(Y_h)^{-1}$ with norm at most $2K$. [F5, step 2.1, given]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $z_*=(x_*,T_*)$ be a phase-fixed nonconstant periodic orbit, let $G$ be its phase-bordered shooting residual, and suppose $DG(z_*)$ is invertible with $\|DG(z_*)^{-1}\|_2\le K_J$. Let a convex validated domain contain the segment from $z_*$ to a candidate $z=(x,T)$, with $\|z-z_*\|_2\le r$, and suppose $DG$ is $L_J$-Lipschitz there and $K_JL_Jr\le1$. If a validated residual box $R$ contains $G(z)$ and $\epsilon\ge\sup_{v\in R}\|v\|_2$, then
$$ \|z-z_*\|_2\le2K_J\epsilon. $$
If the state tube is convex, $\|Df\|_2\le L_f$, $\|f\|_2\le M_f$, and $T,T_*\le T_+$ there, then the scaled trajectories satisfy
$$ \sup_{0\le s\le1}\|\phi_{Ts}(x)-\phi_{T_*s}(x_*)\|_2 \le 2K_J e^{T_+L_f}(1+M_f)\epsilon. $$
The residual box may be taken from [[def-validated-periodic-shooting-jet-enclosure]]. A residual without the stated neighborhood, inverse, and derivative bounds gives no orbit-error conclusion.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A validated local shooting residual and inverse/Lipschitz bounds give orbit/period error and a scaled-trajectory bound only within the supplied neighborhood.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 By [F6], $G$ is $C^2$ on the common validation tube. Put $\delta=z-z_*$. Since $G(z_*)=0$, Taylor's formula [F3] gives $G(z)=DG(z_*)\delta+R_2$ with $\|R_2\|_2\le(L_J/2)\|\delta\|_2^2$. The residual box inclusion [F2] implies $\|G(z)\|_2\le\epsilon$. Multiplying by $DG(z_*)^{-1}$ and using its norm bound yields $\|\delta\|_2\le K_J\epsilon+(K_JL_J/2)\|\delta\|_2^2$. The hypothesis $\|\delta\|_2\le r$ and $K_JL_Jr\le1$ make the quadratic term at most $\frac12\|\delta\|_2$; rearrangement proves $\|\delta\|_2\le2K_J\epsilon$. [F1, F2, F3, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $x(s)=\phi_{Ts}(x)$ and $x_*(s)=\phi_{T_*s}(x_*)$. The chain rule [F5] and the flow equation give their scaled equations and $ \|x'(s)-x_*'(s)\|_2\le T_+L_f\|x(s)-x_*(s)\|_2+M_f|T-T_*|. $ Integrating this inequality and applying [F4] gives $\|x(s)-x_*(s)\|_2\le e^{T_+L_f}(\|x-x_*\|_2+M_f|T-T_*|)$. Each initial-state or period difference is at most $\|\delta\|_2$, so step 1.1 proves the trajectory estimate. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ have an algebraically simple eigenvalue $\lambda_0$, with right vector $v$ normalized by $\|v\|_2=1$ and compatible left vector $w$ normalized by $w^*v=1$. Put $Q=I-vw^*$, $W=\ker w^*$, $q=\|Q\|_2$, and $\kappa=\|w\|_2$. The restriction $A_W=A|_W$ is well-defined. Let $D=\{\lambda:|\lambda-\lambda_0|\le\rho\}$ be a disk such that every $\lambda\in D$ makes $\lambda I_W-A_W$ invertible and
$$R\ge\sup_{\lambda\in D}\| (\lambda I_W-A_W)^{-1}\|_2<\infty.$$
If $n\ge2$, $\|E\|_2\le\delta$, and $Rq^2\delta<1$, then every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A+E$ in $D$ satisfies
$$
|\lambda-\lambda_0|\le \kappa\delta+\frac{\kappa qR\delta^2}{1-Rq^2\delta}.
$$
When $A$ is a monodromy matrix, this bounds the corresponding Floquet multiplier. The formula is a finite nonnormal perturbation enclosure; an unseparated cluster requires the contour-count route instead.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: An isolated simple eigenvalue and a uniform transverse resolvent bound give the stated finite nonnormal perturbation disk radius while the strict denominator remains positive.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 Let $\lambda\in D$ be an eigenvalue of $A+E$ with eigenvector $x=\alpha v+y$, $y\in W$. If $\alpha=0$, projection onto $W$ gives $y=(\lambda I_W-A_W)^{-1}QE y$. Thus $\|y\|_2\le Rq\delta\|y\|_2$, while $Rq\delta\le Rq^2\delta<1$, forcing $y=0$, contrary to $x\ne0$. Hence $\alpha\ne0$; rescale the eigenvector so $\alpha=1$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

4.1 Applying $w^*$ to the same eigen-equation gives $\lambda-\lambda_0=w^*Ev+w^*Ey$. The first term is the first-order eigenvalue derivative [F3]; its modulus is at most $\kappa\delta$, while the second is at most $\kappa\delta\|y\|_2$. Substituting step 3.1 gives the stronger denominator $1-Rq\delta$. Since $q\ge1$, $1-Rq^2\delta\le1-Rq\delta$ and both are positive, so replacing by the smaller denominator yields the stated bound. If $A$ is monodromy, [F5] identifies $\lambda$ as a Floquet multiplier. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface: If [[alg-floquet-multiplier-cluster-certifier]] returns `certified-count(c)` for a nonempty matrix family $\mathcal M$ and a simple positively oriented convex polygon $\Gamma$, then every $M\in\mathcal M$ has exactly $c$ eigenvalues in $\operatorname{int}P$, counted with algebraic multiplicity, and no eigenvalue on $\Gamma$. In particular, this holds for every exact monodromy matrix enclosed by a validated shooting jet whose interval block is contained in $\mathcal M$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A certified contour count assigns the same multiplicity to every matrix in a nonempty enclosed monodromy family and excludes contour eigenvalues.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 3.1 For each fixed $M$, put $p_M(z)=\det(zI-M)$. The boundary is in the resolvent by [F1], so $p_M$ is nonzero on $\Gamma$. By [F2] with $A=zI-M$ and direction $I$, $p_M'(z)/p_M(z)=\operatorname{tr}(zI-M)^{-1}$. Facts [F3]–[F4] therefore identify $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma\operatorname{tr}(zI-M)^{-1}dz$ with the number of eigenvalues inside $P$, counted with algebraic multiplicity; it is an integer from $0$ to $n$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 The successful output places the real part of every such integer strictly inside the half-unit interval around $c$. There is only one integer in that interval, namely $c$. Its imaginary part is zero and is contained by the checked imaginary interval. Hence every $M$ has exactly $c$ interior eigenvalues and none on the resolvent-certified boundary. If a monodromy matrix lies in $\mathcal M$, the same universal statement applies to it. [F5, F6, step 3.1] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface: Let an exact nonconstant phase-fixed periodic orbit and monodromy matrix $M_*$ be supplied by a sound periodic-orbit certificate. Suppose $M_*$ belongs to a matrix family with a certified complete cluster list of pairwise disjoint filled convex polygons $P_0,\ldots,P_s$: each count is certified by [[thm-floquet-multiplier-cluster-certificate-soundness]], the counts sum to the state dimension $d$, $1\in\operatorname{int}P_0$, and the count in $P_0$ is one. Suppose also that for each $j\ge1$, $P_j\subset\{z:|z|\le1-\sigma\}$ for one supplied $\sigma>0$. Then the periodic orbit is orbitally asymptotically stable. If any non-phase cluster enclosure meets or intersects the unit circle, these hypotheses fail and this theorem gives no stability verdict.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A complete disjoint polygon cluster list isolates one neutral phase multiplier and strictly contracts every remaining cluster, yielding orbital asymptotic stability.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 Nonconstancy and flow uniqueness [F6] imply $f(\gamma(0))\ne0$, since otherwise the constant solution through $\gamma(0)$ would be the unique trajectory. Define $H=\{t\in\mathbb R:\gamma(t)=\gamma(0)\}$. Flow uniqueness makes $H$ an additive subgroup: a return to $\gamma(0)$ repeats the entire trajectory, so sums and differences of return times are return times. Continuity makes $H$ closed. One coordinate has nonzero derivative at zero and is strictly monotone on a sufficiently short interval; hence $H$ has no nonzero element there. Its positive infimum $S$ is therefore positive and belongs to $H$ by closedness. For any positive period $T$, division by $S$ gives $T=kS+r$ with integer $k\ge1$ and $0\le r<S$; the subgroup property gives $r\in H$, so minimality forces $r=0$. Thus $T=kS$, where $S$ is the least positive period. [F1, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Let $M_S$ be the monodromy over $S$. By flow composition and the chain rule [F6], $M_*=M_S^k$. The phase tangent is a $1$ eigenvector of $M_S$ by [F2]. If $M_Sv=\alpha v$ with $\alpha^k
e1$, then $M_*v=\alpha^kv$ is a non-phase eigenvalue of $M_*$, so step 1.1 gives $|\alpha|^k<1$ and $|\alpha|<1$. If $\alpha^k=1$ and $\alpha
e1$, then $v$ and the phase tangent are independent eigenvectors of $M_*$ for eigenvalue $1$, contradicting its algebraic simplicity. If $\alpha=1$ and there were an eigenvector independent of the phase tangent, the same contradiction follows. If the eigenvalue $1$ of $M_S$ had a nontrivial Jordan chain, [F6] gives a generalized vector $v$ with $(M_S-I)v=f(\gamma(0))$ after rescaling. Then $(M_* - I)v=(M_S^k-I)v=k f(\gamma(0))
e0$, contradicting the algebraic simplicity of $1$ for $M_*$. Hence $1$ is simple for $M_S$ and every other eigenvalue of $M_S$ is strictly inside the unit circle. [F2, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

On the annulus $U=\{(x,y):1/2<\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<3/2\}$ consider
$$
\dot x=(1-r)x-y,\qquad \dot y=(1-r)y+x,\qquad r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.
$$
The unit circle is an orbitally asymptotically stable periodic orbit of period $2\pi$. At $x_*=(1,0)$ the affine phase $\psi_b(x,y)=x-1$ has a singular phase-bordered shooting Jacobian, while $\psi_g(x,y)=y$ is transverse and gives an invertible phase-bordered shooting Jacobian.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 The identities $\dot r=(xx'+yy')/r$ and $\dot\vartheta=(xy'-yx')/r^2$ give $\dot r=r(1-r)$ and $\dot\vartheta=1$. Thus $r=1$ is invariant and $\vartheta(t)=\vartheta(0)+t$, so the least period is $2\pi$. Differentiating $r(1-r)$ at $r=1$ gives the radial variational equation $\dot\rho=-\rho$, whose multiplier is $e^{-2\pi}<1$; the angular variational equation is $\dot\alpha=0$, whose multiplier is $1$. Because the polar-coordinate Jacobian at times $0$ and $2\pi$ is the same invertible matrix, the Cartesian monodromy is conjugate to $\operatorname{diag}(e^{-2\pi},1)$. For $r<1$ the radial derivative is positive, and for $r>1$ it is negative, so nearby radii move monotonically toward $1$ and cannot leave their initial radial interval. Their distance to the unit circle therefore tends to zero while remaining small. This proves orbital asymptotic stability and shows the neutral multiplier is simple. [given, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $A,E\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be Hermitian, and order their real eigenvalues decreasingly as $\lambda_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(A)$, $\lambda_1(E)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(E)$, and likewise for $A+E$. Then for every $1\le k\le n$,
$$
|\lambda_k(A+E)-\lambda_k(A)|\le\|E\|_2.
$$
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The induced norm of a Hermitian perturbation bounds every ordered eigenvalue displacement, with no eigenvalue simplicity assumption.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Realify $A$ and $E$. Their eigenvalues in decreasing order repeat each complex eigenvalue twice, so the $2k$-th eigenvalue of $\mathcal R(A)$ is $\lambda_k(A)$ and similarly for $E$ and $A+E$. By [F2] with indices $i=2k,j=1$, the upper Weyl inequality gives $\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A+E))\le\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A))+\lambda_1(\mathcal R(E))$. With $i=2k,j=2n$, the lower inequality gives $\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A+E))\ge\lambda_{2k}(\mathcal R(A))+\lambda_{2n}(\mathcal R(E))$. [given, F1, F2]

before.reason: lem-hermitian-block-ldl-inertia-additivity states a one-way implication or a definition, not an equivalence.

after.reason: Statement: This item gives its stated forward implication or definition, not a converse characterizing all its hypotheses. An invertible leading Hermitian block splits inertia into that block and its Schur complement, including a zero-size trailing complement.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $k\ge1$, $m\ge0$, and let $H=\begin{pmatrix}D&B^*\\B&C\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb C^{(k+m)\times(k+m)}$ be Hermitian, where $D=D^*\in\mathbb C^{k\times k}$ is nonsingular, $B\in\mathbb C^{m\times k}$, and $C=C^*\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}$. Define the Schur complement $S=C-BD^{-1}B^*$. Inertia triples are added coordinatewise, and the $0\times0$ matrix has inertia $(0,0,0)$. Then
$$
\operatorname{inertia}(H)=\operatorname{inertia}(D)+\operatorname{inertia}(S),
$$
where the triples are added coordinatewise.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: An invertible leading Hermitian block splits inertia into that block and its Schur complement, including a zero-size trailing complement.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 Since $D=D^*$ and $D$ is invertible, $(D^{-1})^*=(D^*)^{-1}=D^{-1}$. Therefore $(BD^{-1}B^*)^*=BD^{-1}B^*$, and $C=C^*$ gives $S^*=S$. By [F1], $\operatorname{inertia}(H)=\operatorname{inertia}(\operatorname{diag}(D,S))$. If $m=0$, the trailing block is empty and its inertia is $(0,0,0)$ by the stated convention. If $m>0$, [F2] diagonalizes the Hermitian matrices $D$ and $S$ separately; concatenating their orthonormal eigenbases diagonalizes the block diagonal matrix, so its positive, negative and zero counts are the sums of the corresponding counts for $D$ and $S$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

after.reason: Statement: This item gives its stated forward implication or definition, not a converse characterizing all its hypotheses. Set inclusion for the whole matrix/right-hand-side family gives existence in the supplied box; a separate strict contraction bound gives uniqueness for each fixed pair.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $\mathcal b\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be nonempty, let $X$ be a nonempty closed complex rectangle box in $\mathbb C^n\cong\mathbb R^{2n}$, let $x_0\in X$, and let the point matrix $R$ be nonsingular. For each fixed $A\in\mathcal A,b\in\mathcal b$, define
$$
\Phi_{A,b}(x)=x-R(Ax-b)
$$
and
$$
K^*(X)=\{x_0-R(Ax_0-b)+(I-RA)(x-x_0): A\in\mathcal A,\ b\in\mathcal b,\ x\in X\}.
$$
If $K^*(X)\subseteq X$, then every admitted pair $(A,b)$ has a solution in $X$. If in addition a number $q<1$ satisfies $\|I-RA\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le q$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$, that solution is unique in $X$ for each fixed pair.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Set inclusion for the whole matrix/right-hand-side family gives existence in the supplied box; a separate strict contraction bound gives uniqueness for each fixed pair.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Fix any $A\in\mathcal A,b\in\mathcal b$. Algebra gives $\Phi_{A,b}(x)=x_0-R(Ax_0-b)+(I-RA)(x-x_0)$, so $K^*(X)\subseteq X$ implies $\Phi_{A,b}(X)\subseteq X$. The affine map $\Phi_{A,b}$ is continuous on the closed box, so [F1] gives a fixed point $x\in X$. Since $R$ is nonsingular, $\Phi_{A,b}(x)=x$ is equivalent to $Ax=b$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 If $x,y\in X$ both solve the same system, then both are fixed points and $x-y=(I-RA)(x-y)$. By [F2] and [F3], $\|x-y\|_\infty\le q\|x-y\|_\infty$. Since the vector infinity norm [F3] vanishes only at the zero vector and $q<1$, $x=y$. This proves uniqueness for that pair; the pair was arbitrary. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

before.reason: thm-near-orthonormal-hermitian-eigenvalue-enclosure states a one-way implication or a definition, not an equivalence.

after.reason: Statement: This item gives its stated forward implication or definition, not a converse characterizing all its hypotheses. A residual/orthogonality certificate gives uniform ordered Hermitian eigenvalue intervals after sorting the approximate diagonal values.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $(V,\Theta,\delta,\rho,M_A,M_\Theta,\tau)$ be a residual and orthogonality certificate for a nonempty family $\mathcal A$ of Hermitian matrices in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Sort the diagonal entries of $\Theta$ increasingly as $\theta_{(1)}\le\cdots\le\theta_{(n)}$. Then every $A\in\mathcal A$ has ordered eigenvalues $\lambda_1(A)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(A)$ satisfying
$$
|\lambda_k(A)-\theta_{(k)}|\le \rho+(M_A+M_\Theta)\tau,\qquad 1\le k\le n.
$$
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A residual/orthogonality certificate gives uniform ordered Hermitian eigenvalue intervals after sorting the approximate diagonal values.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 Set $Q=VH^{-1}$. Then $Q^*Q=H^{-1}V^*VH^{-1}=I$. Thus $Q$ is injective and [F4] makes the square matrix $Q$ invertible, so $Q$ is unitary. The eigenvalues of $H$ lie between $\sqrt{1-\delta}$ and $\sqrt{1+\delta}$, hence $\|V-Q\|_2=\|Q(H-I)\|_2=\|H-I\|_2\le1-\sqrt{1-\delta}\le\tau$. For the upper deviation, $\sqrt{1+\delta}-1\le1-\sqrt{1-\delta}$ because $\sqrt{1+\delta}+\sqrt{1-\delta}\le2$. Unitary invariance in [F5] justifies the norm equality. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each $A\in\mathcal A$, the residual identity $AQ-Q\Theta=A(Q-V)+(AV-V\Theta)+(V-Q)\Theta$ and certificate bounds give $\|AQ-Q\Theta\|_2\le M_A\tau+\rho+\tau M_\Theta=\eta$. By the triangle inequality and submultiplicativity [F7], each product term in the identity is bounded by its factor norms, giving the displayed estimate. Since $Q$ is unitary, [F5] gives that $Q^*AQ$ has the same ordered eigenvalues as $A$ and, using [F7], $\|Q^*AQ-\Theta\|_2=\|Q^*(AQ-Q\Theta)\|_2\le\eta$. [given, F5, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Gamma$ be a nonempty finite union of closed line segments in $\mathbb C$, let $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be nonempty, and let $A_0\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Each segment of $\Gamma$ is assigned to one of finitely many disks $D_j=\{z:|z-z_j|\le r_j\}$ whose radius is $r_j\ge0$ and whose disk contains both endpoints of that segment. For each disk there are $R_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and nonnegative bounds $e_j,\delta_A,s_j$ satisfying
$$e_j\ge\|I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad \delta_A\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad s_j\ge\|R_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$
If $q_j=e_j+s_j(r_j+\delta_A)<1$ for each $j$, then every $z\in\Gamma$ and $A\in\mathcal A$ make $zI-A$ invertible, and
$$\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \max_j\frac{s_j}{1-q_j}.$$
The theorem bounds the resolvent on the supplied contour cover; it does not count enclosed eigenvalues or certify a nonnormal eigenvalue disk from a residual.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Endpoint-covered contour segments and strict disk Neumann bounds certify uniform resolvent invertibility and norm, without counting interior eigenvalues.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.2 Fix a disk, $z\in D_j$, and $A\in\mathcal A$. The exact identity $I-R_j(zI-A)=I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)-R_j\bigl((z-z_j)I-(A-A_0)\bigr)$ and [F2] give $\|I-R_j(zI-A)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le e_j+s_j(|z-z_j|+\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C})\le q_j<1$. [F1] applies to $M=R_j(zI-A)=I-E$ with $E=I-M$, giving $\|M^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le(1-q_j)^{-1}$. Here [F4] gives $\|(z-z_j)I\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}=|z-z_j|$, and the row-sum norm's triangle inequality and compatibility [F2, F4] justify the defect estimate. [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], $\|I\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}=1$. Since $M=R_j(zI-A)$ is nonsingular, both square factors are nonsingular by [F3]. Then $(zI-A)^{-1}=M^{-1}R_j$, so [F2] gives $\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le s_j/(1-q_j)$. The disk cover from step 1.1 yields the maximum bound on all of $\Gamma$, uniformly in $A$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
The real family
$$
\mathcal A=\left\{A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\t&1\end{pmatrix}:-1\le t\le1\right\}
$$
is represented by the entrywise interval box with off-diagonal entries $[-1,1]$. It contains a singular matrix, and its natural Leibniz interval evaluation $[0,2]$ does not certify uniform nonsingularity.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The two-by-two off-diagonal interval family includes singular endpoint members and its Leibniz interval straddles zero, preventing a uniform nonsingularity verdict.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For each $t\in[-1,1]$, $\det A(t)=1-t^2\in[0,1]$. The direct interval product $[-1,1]\cdot[-1,1]=[-1,1]$ encloses $t^2$, so the Leibniz interval expression $1-[-1,1]=[0,2]$ contains every determinant. At $t=1$, $A(1)(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}=0$ with a nonzero vector, so $A(1)$ is singular. The interval $[0,2]$ includes zero and is not $\{0\}$; [F1] therefore makes no uniform nonsingularity claim from this enclosure. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 If uniform residual data with $q<1$ existed for this whole family and any nonempty right-hand-side set, [F2] would make $A(1)$ invertible. This contradicts the nonzero null vector just exhibited. Hence such a usable uniform residual certificate cannot hold for the family. [given, F2, step 1.1, contradiction] ∎

\lambda_1(A)\in[-9/8,-3/4],\qquad \lambda_2(A)\in[15/8,9/4].

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $X,Y$ be nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces and
let $\Psi:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be an extended-real function. A
pair $(x_*,y_*)$ is a
**saddle point** of $\Psi$ if $\Psi(x_*,y_*)$ is finite and
$$\Psi(x_*,y)\le \Psi(x_*,y_*)\le \Psi(x,y_*)\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).$$
The inequalities must be defined at the arguments they display. For an
equality-constrained problem the primal set may be a product set of
finite-valued pairs $(x,z)$.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $T:E\to E$ be firmly nonexpansive on $E=\mathbb R^n$, suppose
$\operatorname{Fix}(T)=\{p:T(p)=p\}$ is nonempty, and start at any $w_0$.
Then the Picard sequence $w_{k+1}=T(w_k)$ converges to a fixed point of $T$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Firm nonexpansiveness and a supplied fixed point make the finite-dimensional Picard sequence converge; its zero-dimensional space is handled directly as the singleton.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 If $n=0$, [F3] gives $E=\{0\}$ and the nonempty fixed-point set forces $T(0)=0$; since $w_0=0$, every iterate equals the fixed point. It remains to consider $n\ge1$. Firm nonexpansiveness applied to $w_k$ and a fixed point $p$ gives $\|w_{k+1}-p\|_2^2\le\langle w_{k+1}-p,w_k-p\rangle$. Expanding $w_k-p=(w_{k+1}-p)+(w_k-w_{k+1})$ and rearranging yields $$\|w_{k+1}-p\|_2^2+\|w_{k+1}-w_k\|_2^2\le\|w_k-p\|_2^2.$$ Summing this inequality shows that the distances to $p$ are nonincreasing, the sequence is bounded, and $\sum_k\|w_{k+1}-w_k\|_2^2<\infty$, so the increments tend to zero. [A1, given, F1, F3, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $E=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean norm, let $D\subseteq E$, and let
$T:D\to E$ satisfy $\|T(p)-T(p')\|_2\le\|p-p'\|_2$ for all $p,p'\in D$.
For every $y\in E$ there exists $q\in E$ such that
$$\|q-T(p)\|_2\le\|y-p\|_2\qquad(p\in D).$$
Equivalently, one value can be added at the new input $y$ without violating
the Lipschitz constant $1$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: A nonexpansive map on an arbitrary subset admits one further Lipschitz-compatible value; empty input domain and zero-dimensional ambient space have explicit direct branches.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 If $n=0$, then $E=\{0\}$. If $D$ is empty choose $q=0$; if it is nonempty then $D=\{0\}$, $y=p=T(p)=0$, and $q=0$ satisfies the inequality. Hence assume $n\ge1$. If $D=\varnothing$, any $q$ works. Otherwise consider any finite nonempty list $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in D$ and set $$h_i(q)=\|q-Tp_i\|_2^2-\|y-p_i\|_2^2,\qquad H(q)=\max_{1\le i\le m}h_i(q).$$ The continuous function $H$ is coercive because each $h_i(q)\to+\infty$ as $\|q\|_2\to\infty$. A nonempty sublevel $\{H\le H(0)\}$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F2]; [F3] gives a global minimizer $q_0$ of $H$. [A1, given, F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 Let $I=\{i:h_i(q_0)=H(q_0)\}$ be the nonempty active set. If $0$ were not in the convex hull of the finitely many gradients $2(q_0-Tp_i)$, $i\in I$, project $0$ onto that compact convex hull using [F4]. The projection vector $v\ne0$ obeys $\langle v,2(q_0-Tp_i)\rangle\ge\|v\|_2^2$ for each $i\in I$, by the variational inequality. For sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, every active $h_i(q_0-\epsilon v)$ decreases strictly; the finitely many inactive terms have a strict gap below $H(q_0)$ and remain below it by continuity. This contradicts minimality. Therefore there are weights $\alpha_i\ge0$, supported on $I$, with $\sum_i\alpha_i=1$ and $q_0=\sum_i\alpha_i T p_i$. [A1, F1, F4, step 1.1, contradiction, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
For proper closed convex $f_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, linear
$A_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to\mathbb R^p$, data $b\in\mathbb R^p$, penalty
$\rho>0$, and scaled multiplier $u^k$, the **naive sequential three-block
ADMM** sweep is
$$x_1^{k+1}\in\arg\min_{x_1}f_1(x_1)+\frac\rho2\|A_1x_1+A_2x_2^k+A_3x_3^k-b+u^k\|^2,$$
then $x_2^{k+1}$ minimizes the same augmented residual with $x_1^{k+1}$,
$x_2$ variable and $x_3^k$ fixed; then $x_3^{k+1}$ minimizes it with the
first two new blocks; finally
$$u^{k+1}=u^k+A_1x_1^{k+1}+A_2x_2^{k+1}+A_3x_3^{k+1}-b.$$
Only exact attained block minimizers advance the state. A finite solver must
return an explicit failed or cap-exhausted status if it cannot certify a
minimizer. This is a definition of a procedure and asserts no convergence.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, let
$K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be linear,
let $c\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\rho>0$. The primal problem is
$$\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to }Kx+Lz=c,$$
and its Lagrangian is
$\mathcal L((x,z),y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle$.
A saddle point means a saddle pair in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]].

For an exact outer sweep with scaled dual $u^k$, compute, in order,
$$x^{k+1}\in\arg\min_x\left(f(x)+\frac\rho2\|Kx+Lz^k-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
$$z^{k+1}\in\arg\min_z\left(g(z)+\frac\rho2\|Kx^{k+1}+Lz-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
then set $r^{k+1}=Kx^{k+1}+Lz^{k+1}-c$ and
$u^{k+1}=u^k+r^{k+1}$. Report also the unscaled dual
$y^k=\rho u^k$, objective $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$, and primal residual $r^k$.
If an exact subproblem has multiple minimizers, choose the unique minimum-norm
member of its nonempty closed convex minimizer set; existence and uniqueness of
that tie-break follow from [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]].

A finite implementation supplies finite inner iteration caps for both solves.
A solve is accepted only with a certificate of an attained global minimizer
before its cap. Return **invalid-input** for invalid dimensions or $\rho\le0$;
return **x-solve-failed**, **x-cap-exhausted**, **z-solve-failed**, or
**z-cap-exhausted** if the corresponding solve fails, is uncertified, or reaches
its cap. A failed sweep does not change the outer state, even if its first
subproblem was solved. These statuses give no approximate convergence guarantee.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Each exact attained block solution uses the unique minimum-norm minimizer tie-break; a failed finite second solve does not commit even a successfully computed first block.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For either block write its subproblem objective as $F(v)+Q(v)$, where $F$ is $f$ or $g$ and $Q$ is the finite continuous convex residual quadratic from [F2]. Its epigraph is the inverse image of the closed set $\operatorname{epi}F$ under the continuous map $(v,s)\mapsto(v,s-Q(v))$, so it is closed by [F1]. If its minimum is attained, the minimum value $a$ is finite: properness gives a finite competitor and neither summand takes $-\infty$. Its minimizer set is nonempty and equals $\{v:F(v)+Q(v)\le a\}$, the inverse image of that closed epigraph under $v\mapsto(v,a)$, hence is closed. The sum of the two convex functions is convex; at two minimizers, convexity bounds every segment value by $a$, while minimality bounds it below by $a$. Thus the minimizer set is convex. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For either block, if its dimension is zero then [F4] makes its Euclidean space the singleton $\{0\}$, so the nonempty minimizer set in step 1.1 is that singleton and its minimum-norm member is unique. In positive dimension, [F3] gives a unique point nearest the origin in the nonempty closed convex minimizer set. Thus the specified tie-break exists and is unique in every dimension, so exact outer sweeps are deterministic. A capped solver that does not certify this attained minimizer returns its stated failure status without changing $(x^k,z^k,u^k)$; hence the finite wrapper makes no claim that every cap will succeed. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is the
extended-real function on the same Euclidean space
$$f^*(s):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}.$$
When $f(x)=+\infty$, the corresponding term is $-\infty$ and does not increase
the supremum. Its effective domain is
$\operatorname{dom}f^*=\{s:f^*(s)<+\infty\}$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The extended-real conjugate is a supremum over the Euclidean domain, with infinite primal values contributing negative infinity rather than undefined subtraction.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $A$ be maximal monotone on $E=\mathbb R^n$ and let $\rho>0$. For every
$y\in E$ there is a unique $x\in E$ with $y-x\in\rho A(x)$. Thus the
resolvent from [[def-resolvent-of-a-monotone-relation]] is an everywhere-defined
map and, for all $y,y'\in E$,
$$\|J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y'\|_2^2\le \langle J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y',y-y'\rangle.$$
This is firm nonexpansiveness; it also implies the map is 1-Lipschitz.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Maximality and one-point extension give a unique resolvent at every Euclidean input, and monotonicity gives its firm norm inequality.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Transform every graph pair $(x,a)\in A$ into $p=x+\rho a$ and $q=x-\rho a$. If two graph pairs are used, then $$\|q-q'\|_2^2\le\|p-p'\|_2^2,$$ because the difference of the right and left sides is $4\rho\langle x-x',a-a'\rangle\ge0$ by [F1]. Also, if $p=p'$, this inequality forces $q=q'$. Thus the rule $T(p)=q$ is a well-defined 1-Lipschitz map on its range $D=\{x+\rho a:(x,a)\in A\}$. [A1, F1, construct, algebra]

3.1 If $x,x'$ both satisfy $y-x\in\rho A(x)$ and $y-x'\in\rho A(x')$, monotonicity gives $0\le\langle x-x',(y-x)-(y-x')\rangle=-\|x-x'\|_2^2$. Thus $x=x'$, so the resolvent is single-valued. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $X=\mathbb R^n$, $Y=\mathbb R^m$, let $f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, and let $K:X\to Y$ be
linear. Its unique adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$ exists by
[[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]], including zero-dimensional
spaces. Identify $K$ with its matrix in the standard Euclidean bases when using
the induced matrix norm below. The primal problem is $\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)$, with saddle function
$$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),$$
where $g^*$ is defined by [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]].
The saddle function $\Phi$ is evaluated on
$\operatorname{dom}f\times\operatorname{dom}g^*$, where both function values
are finite; no undefined extended-real subtraction is used outside this domain.
Assume $\tau,\sigma>0$ and
$\tau\sigma\|K\|_2^2<1$, where $\|K\|_2$ is the induced Euclidean operator
norm of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. Starting from $x^0,y^0$ and
$\bar x^0=x^0$, the exact recurrence is
$$y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^*y^{k+1}),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.$$
In positive-dimensional spaces the proximal maps are everywhere single-valued
by [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; in a
zero-dimensional space its sole input and output are the zero vector, so that
proximal call is single-valued directly. The proper closed convexity of $g^*$
follows from [[lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-convex]]. A finite implementation
uses finite call caps and advances an iterate only after both exact proximal
outputs are certified; otherwise it returns **prox-call-failed** or
**prox-cap-exhausted** and makes no convergence claim for that run.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The two proximal outputs and extrapolated primal point define PDHG under the strict positive-step norm product, with zero-dimensional proximal calls explicitly single-valued.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 By [F1] and [F3], both proximal inputs in the recurrence are proper closed convex functions; [F2] supplies the defining conjugate expression for the dual term. If a proximal space has positive dimension, [F4] gives an everywhere unique output. If it is zero-dimensional, [F7] makes it the singleton $\{0\}$ and properness gives the unique zero output directly. Since $\tau,\sigma>0$, every exact update exists uniquely, including when $K=0$; the strict step inequality then reads $0<1$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F7, given]

2.1 The three assignments fully specify the exact state and extrapolated value; $K^*$ in the primal update is the adjoint of [F6], and the step-size condition uses the induced norm [F5]. If either finite routine fails to certify its exact proximal output before its cap, the state is not advanced and the status is not a convergence certificate. The recurrence makes no pointwise convergence claim. [A1, F5, F6, given, F4, given] ∎

Suppose proper closed convex $f,g$ have a saddle point $(x_*,z_*,y_*)$ for the
Lagrangian in [[alg-two-block-admm-scaled]], with $Kx_*+Lz_*=c$, and every
subproblem in the exact ADMM sequence is attained. Put
$\Delta z^{k+1}=z^{k+1}-z^k$ and
$$V^k=\frac1\rho\|y^k-y_*\|_2^2+\rho\|L(z^k-z_*)\|_2^2.$$
For every $k\ge1$,
$$V^{k+1}\le V^k-\rho\|r^{k+1}\|_2^2-\rho\|L\Delta z^{k+1}\|_2^2.$$
The index begins at $k=1$: an arbitrary initial $z^0$ need not satisfy a
previous $z$-subproblem optimality condition. Also, with $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$
and $p_*=f(x_*)+g(z_*)$, every exact sweep satisfies
$$p_{k+1}-p_*\le-\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle+ \rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},r^{k+1}-L(z^{k+1}-z_*)\rangle,$$
$$p_*-p_{k+1}\le\langle y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle.$$

$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)$. For every

$$\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\Phi(x^{k+1},y)-\Phi(x,y^{k+1})\bigr) \le\frac{\|x-x^0\|_2^2}{2\tau}+\frac{\|y-y^0\|_2^2}{2\sigma}.$$

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For each positive-dimensional proximal space, the optimality condition [F2] and extended-real subgradient definition [F3] give the relevant inequality. If a proximal space is zero-dimensional, [F6] says its only point is $0$; its update and test point are both $0$, so the same inequality is equality in that coordinate. Therefore in every dimension the two inequalities are $$g^*(y)-g^*(y^{k+1})\ge\left\langle\frac{y^k-y^{k+1}}\sigma+K\bar x^k,y-y^{k+1}\right\rangle,$$ $$f(x)-f(x^{k+1})\ge\left\langle\frac{x^k-x^{k+1}}\tau-K^*y^{k+1},x-x^{k+1}\right\rangle.$$ The identity $-\langle a-b,c-b\rangle=(\|c-a\|^2-\|c-b\|^2-\|b-a\|^2)/2$ applied to the primal and dual displacement terms gives the two distance differences $E_k-E_{k+1}-X_{k+1}$ and $E_k-E_{k+1}-Y_{k+1}$ in their respective coordinates. The bilinear terms from the primal inequality and the gap expand as $\langle y^{k+1},K(x-x^{k+1})\rangle+\langle Kx^{k+1},y\rangle-\langle Kx,y^{k+1}\rangle=\langle Kx^{k+1},y-y^{k+1}\rangle$. Adding the dual update term $\langle K\bar x^k,y^{k+1}-y\rangle$ gives $\langle K(\bar x^k-x^{k+1}),y^{k+1}-y\rangle$ in the upper bound for $G_{k+1}$. Moving this term to the other side yields $$E_k\ge G_{k+1}+E_{k+1}+X_{k+1}+Y_{k+1}+\langle K(x^{k+1}-\bar x^k),y^{k+1}-y\rangle,$$ where $G_{k+1}=\Phi(x^{k+1},y)-\Phi(x,y^{k+1})$, $E_j=\|x-x^j\|^2/(2\tau)+\|y-y^j\|^2/(2\sigma)$, $X_j=\|x^j-x^{j-1}\|^2/(2\tau)$, and $Y_j=\|y^j-y^{j-1}\|^2/(2\sigma)$. [[alg-two-block-admm-scaled]]. Suppose $f,g$ are proper closed convex, a
Lagrangian saddle point $(x_*,z_*,y_*)$ exists, $\rho>0$, and every outer
subproblem is attained exactly. Write $p_*=f(x_*)+g(z_*)$. Then
$$r^k\to0,\qquad f(x^k)+g(z^k)\to p_*,\qquad y^k\to\bar y$$
for some dual optimum $\bar y$ of
$d(y)=\inf_{x,z}\mathcal L((x,z),y)$. The theorem does not assert convergence

selected_current_proof_blocks: 2.1 Fixing $z=z_*$ and then $x=x_*$ in the right saddle inequality gives $-K^*y_*\in\partial f(x_*)$ and $-L^*y_*\in\partial g(z_*)$. By [F6], $f(x_*)+f^*(-K^*y_*)=-\langle y_*,Kx_*\rangle,\qquad g(z_*)+g^*(-L^*y_*)=-\langle y_*,Lz_*\rangle.$ Each component infimum is below a finite value because $f,g$ are proper, so neither equals $+\infty$. If both are finite, choosing independent points within any $\epsilon>0$ of them proves that the joint infimum is their sum; if either is $-\infty$, fixing a finite competitor in the other block and sending the first block value down shows the joint infimum is $-\infty$. Thus separating the $x$ and $z$ infima and using [F4] gives the extended-real identity $$d(y)=-f^*(-K^*y)-g^*(-L^*y)-\langle y,c\rangle.$$ The terms are well-defined because [F5] excludes $-\infty$ conjugate values. Substituting the two equalities and feasibility into the formula gives $d(y_*)=p_*$. The dual solution set $Y_*:=\{y:d(y)=p_*\}$ is nonempty. Weak duality gives $d(y)\le p_*$, so $y\in Y_*$ iff $\mathcal L((x,z),y)\ge p_*$ for every $x,z$. Each finite-valued pair $(x,z)$ imposes a closed affine half-space in $y$; an infinite-valued pair imposes no restriction. Thus $Y_*$ is closed and convex as an intersection of closed convex sets. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra, algebra]

5.1 If $p=0$, then $\mathbb R^p=\{0\}$ by [F10], so $y^k=0$ for every $k$; step 2.1 shows this unique dual vector is optimal, and dual convergence follows. Assume henceforth $p\ge1$. Boundedness from step 2.2 and [F7] give at least one dual cluster point. Let $y_1,y_2\in Y_*$ be any two cluster points. Each pairs with the same primal optimizer to form a saddle point, so [F3] makes both energy sequences $$V^k(y_i)=\rho^{-1}\|y^k-y_i\|_2^2+\rho\|L(z^k-z_*)\|_2^2\quad(i=1,2)$$ nonincreasing from $k=1$ and bounded below; each therefore converges. Expanding the two squared norms gives $V^k(y_1)-V^k(y_2)=\frac2\rho\langle y^k,y_2-y_1\rangle+\frac{\|y_1\|_2^2-\|y_2\|_2^2}{\rho},$ so $\langle y^k,y_2-y_1\rangle$ converges. Along subsequences tending to $y_1$ and $y_2$ the limits are equal, so $\langle y_1-y_2,y_2-y_1\rangle=-\|y_1-y_2\|_2^2=0$ and $y_1=y_2$. [A1, F3, F7, F10, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra]

If both are finite, choosing independent points within any $\epsilon>0$ of them proves that the joint infimum is their sum; if either is $-\infty$, fixing a finite competitor in the other block and sending the first block value down shows the joint infimum is $-\infty$. source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Assume the hypotheses of [[alg-pdhg-primal-dual-hybrid-gradient]] and that
$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)$ has a saddle point
$(x_*,y_*)$ in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]]. For $N\ge1$ define
$$\bar x_N=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}x^{k+1},\qquad \bar y_N=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}y^{k+1}.$$
For every $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, $y\in\operatorname{dom}g^*$,
$$\Phi(\bar x_N,y)-\Phi(x,\bar y_N) \le\frac1N\left(\frac{\|x-x^0\|_2^2}{2\tau} +\frac{\|y-y^0\|_2^2}{2\sigma}\right).$$
In particular, the saddle gap
$\Phi(\bar x_N,y_*)-\Phi(x_*,\bar y_N)$ is nonnegative and obeys this bound
with $(x,y)=(x_*,y_*)$. On bounded test sets the displayed upper bound is
$O(1/N)$. This is an ergodic gap statement; it is not a pointwise objective
bound and does not assert pointwise iterate convergence.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Use three scalar blocks, zero objectives, $\rho=1$, and the homogeneous
constraint $Ax=0$ with
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&1&2\\1&2&2\end{pmatrix}.$$
The sequential three-block recurrence of
[[alg-naive-sequential-three-block-admm]] has a rational initial state for
which its iterates are unbounded, although the unique primal-dual solution is
zero and every block subproblem is attained uniquely.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Three zero-objective scalar blocks have unique attained updates and unique zero primal/dual solution, yet one rational start has an unbounded recurrence.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.2 For state $s^k=(x_2^k,x_3^k,u_1^k,u_2^k,u_3^k)^T$, exact differentiation of the three scalar subproblems gives $x_1^{k+1}=-\frac{a_1^T(u^k+a_2x_2^k+a_3x_3^k)}3$, $x_2^{k+1}=-\frac{a_2^T(u^k+a_1x_1^{k+1}+a_3x_3^k)}6$, and $x_3^{k+1}=-\frac{a_3^T(u^k+a_1x_1^{k+1}+a_2x_2^{k+1})}9$. Substitute these into $u^{k+1}=u^k+a_1x_1^{k+1}+a_2x_2^{k+1}+a_3x_3^{k+1}$; exact rational simplification gives $s^{k+1}=Ms^k$ with $$M=\frac1{162}\begin{pmatrix}144&-9&9&9&-18\\8&157&5&-13&8\\-64&-122&122&-58&-64\\-56&35&-35&91&-56\\88&26&-26&-62&88\end{pmatrix}.$$ The vector $v=(0,0,1,1,1)^T$ satisfies $Mv=0$. Exact rational matrix multiplication gives $p_1=\operatorname{tr}(M)=\frac{301}{81}$, $p_2=\operatorname{tr}(M^2)=\frac{20860}{6561}$, $p_3=\operatorname{tr}(M^3)=\frac{2588159}{1062882}$, and $p_4=\operatorname{tr}(M^4)=\frac{132553799}{86093442}$. Newton's identities $e_1=p_1$, $e_2=(p_1^2-p_2)/2$, $e_3=(p_3-e_1p_2+e_2p_1)/3$, and $e_4=(-p_4+e_1p_3-e_2p_2+e_3p_1)/4$ give $e_1=301/81$, $e_2=287/54$, $e_3=280/81$, $e_4=70/81$; $Mv=0$ gives $e_5=\det M=0$. Therefore $\det(\lambda I-M)=\lambda q(\lambda)$, where $q(\lambda)=\lambda^4-\frac{301}{81}\lambda^3+\frac{287}{54}\lambda^2-\frac{280}{81}\lambda+\frac{70}{81}$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $z=e^{it}$, direct expansion gives $\operatorname{Im}(e^{-2it}q(e^{it}))=\frac{\sin t(22\cos t-21)}{81}$. If this vanishes because $\sin t=0$, substitution gives $q(1)=1/162$ and $q(-1)=775/54$, both nonzero. Otherwise $\cos t=21/22$, and substitution into the real part gives $\operatorname{Re}(e^{-2it}q(e^{it}))=19/19602\ne0$. Thus $q$ has no unit-circle zero. [A1, step 1.2, algebra, cases]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Gamma$ be a nonempty finite union of closed line segments in $\mathbb C$, let $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be nonempty, and let $A_0\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Each segment of $\Gamma$ is assigned to one of finitely many disks $D_j=\{z:|z-z_j|\le r_j\}$ whose radius is $r_j\ge0$ and whose disk contains both endpoints of that segment. For each disk there are $R_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and nonnegative bounds $e_j,\delta_A,s_j$ satisfying
$$e_j\ge\|I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad \delta_A\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad s_j\ge\|R_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$
If $q_j=e_j+s_j(r_j+\delta_A)<1$ for each $j$, then every $z\in\Gamma$ and $A\in\mathcal A$ make $zI-A$ invertible, and
$$\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \max_j\frac{s_j}{1-q_j}.$$
The theorem bounds the resolvent on the supplied contour cover; it does not count enclosed eigenvalues or certify a nonnormal eigenvalue disk from a residual.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Gamma$ be a nonempty finite union of closed line segments in $\mathbb C$, let $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be nonempty, and let $A_0\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Each segment of $\Gamma$ is assigned to one of finitely many disks $D_j=\{z:|z-z_j|\le r_j\}$ whose radius is $r_j\ge0$ and whose disk contains both endpoints of that segment. For each disk there are $R_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and nonnegative bounds $e_j,\delta_A,s_j$ satisfying
$$e_j\ge\|I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad \delta_A\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad s_j\ge\|R_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$
If $q_j=e_j+s_j(r_j+\delta_A)<1$ for each $j$, then every $z\in\Gamma$ and $A\in\mathcal A$ make $zI-A$ invertible, and
$$\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \max_j\frac{s_j}{1-q_j}.$$
The theorem bounds the resolvent on the supplied contour cover; it does not count enclosed eigenvalues or certify a nonnormal eigenvalue disk from a residual.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Endpoint-covered contour segments and strict disk Neumann bounds certify uniform resolvent invertibility and norm, without counting interior eigenvalues.

[given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

For $Z=X+iY\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with real $X,Y$, define its realification
$$
\mathcal R(Z)=\begin{pmatrix}X&-Y\\Y&X\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2n\times2n}.
$$
Then $\mathcal R(ZW)=\mathcal R(Z)\mathcal R(W)$, $\mathcal R(Z^*)=\mathcal R(Z)^{\mathsf T}$, and $Z$ is invertible exactly when $\mathcal R(Z)$ is invertible. If $H=H^*$ is Hermitian with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$ counted with multiplicity, then $\mathcal R(H)$ is real symmetric with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n,\lambda_n$. For any complex matrix $E$, $\|\mathcal R(E)\|_2=\|E\|_2$.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
For $Z=X+iY\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with real $X,Y$, define its realification
$$
\mathcal R(Z)=\begin{pmatrix}X&-Y\\Y&X\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2n\times2n}.
$$
Then $\mathcal R(ZW)=\mathcal R(Z)\mathcal R(W)$, $\mathcal R(Z^*)=\mathcal R(Z)^{\mathsf T}$, and $Z$ is invertible exactly when $\mathcal R(Z)$ is invertible. If $H=H^*$ is Hermitian with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$ counted with multiplicity, then $\mathcal R(H)$ is real symmetric with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n,\lambda_n$. For any complex matrix $E$, $\|\mathcal R(E)\|_2=\|E\|_2$.

$$e_j\ge\|I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad \delta_A\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad s_j\ge\|R_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$

$$\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \max_j\frac{s_j}{1-q_j}.$$

Each segment of $\Gamma$ is assigned to one of finitely many disks $D_j=\{z:|z-z_j|\le r_j\}$ whose radius is $r_j\ge0$ and whose disk contains both endpoints of that segment. $$e_j\ge\|I-R_j(z_jI-A_0)\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad \delta_A\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|A-A_0\|_{\infty,\mathbb C},\quad s_j\ge\|R_j\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}.$$

$$\|(zI-A)^{-1}\|_{\infty,\mathbb C}\le \max_j\frac{s_j}{1-q_j}.$$

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and the Euclidean space $E=\mathbb R^n$ with inner
product and norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A **relation** $A$ on
$E$ is a subset of $E\times E$; write $a\in A(x)$ exactly when
$(x,a)\in A$. Its graph is this subset. The relation is **monotone** if
$$\langle x-x',a-a'\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for all }(x,a),(x',a')\in A.$$
It is **maximal monotone** if it is monotone and no strictly larger subset of
$E\times E$ is monotone. This definition is finite-dimensional and makes no
claim about infinite-dimensional spaces.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Monotonicity quantifies graph pairs in a finite-dimensional Euclidean relation; maximality forbids any larger monotone graph rather than assuming every relation has full domain.

$$\Psi(x_*,y)\le \Psi(x_*,y_*)\le \Psi(x,y_*)\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).$$
The inequalities must be defined at the arguments they display. For an
equality-constrained problem the primal set may be a product set of
finite-valued pairs $(x,z)$.

$\operatorname{Fix}(T)=\{p:T(p)=p\}$ is nonempty, and start at any $w_0$.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 If $n=0$, [F3] gives $E=\{0\}$ and the nonempty fixed-point set forces $T(0)=0$; since $w_0=0$, every iterate equals the fixed point. It remains to consider $n\ge1$. Firm nonexpansiveness applied to $w_k$ and a fixed point $p$ gives $\|w_{k+1}-p\|_2^2\le\langle w_{k+1}-p,w_k-p\rangle$. Expanding $w_k-p=(w_{k+1}-p)+(w_k-w_{k+1})$ and rearranging yields $$\|w_{k+1}-p\|_2^2+\|w_{k+1}-w_k\|_2^2\le\|w_k-p\|_2^2.$$ Summing this inequality shows that the distances to $p$ are nonincreasing, the sequence is bounded, and $\sum_k\|w_{k+1}-w_k\|_2^2<\infty$, so the increments tend to zero. [A1, given, F1, F3, algebra]

3.1 Apply the inequality of step 1.1 with the fixed point $\bar w$ in place of $p$. The distances $\|w_k-\bar w\|_2$ are nonincreasing, and along the subsequence $k_j$ they tend to zero. $$\|q-T(p)\|_2\le\|y-p\|_2\qquad(p\in D).$$

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 If $n=0$, then $E=\{0\}$. If $D$ is empty choose $q=0$; if it is nonempty then $D=\{0\}$, $y=p=T(p)=0$, and $q=0$ satisfies the inequality. Hence assume $n\ge1$. Otherwise consider any finite nonempty list $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in D$ and set $$h_i(q)=\|q-Tp_i\|_2^2-\|y-p_i\|_2^2,\qquad H(q)=\max_{1\le i\le m}h_i(q).$$ The continuous function $H$ is coercive because each $h_i(q)\to+\infty$ as $\|q\|_2\to\infty$. source_evidence.full_current_interface:
For proper closed convex $f_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, linear
$A_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to\mathbb R^p$, data $b\in\mathbb R^p$, penalty
$\rho>0$, and scaled multiplier $u^k$, the **naive sequential three-block
ADMM** sweep is
$$x_1^{k+1}\in\arg\min_{x_1}f_1(x_1)+\frac\rho2\|A_1x_1+A_2x_2^k+A_3x_3^k-b+u^k\|^2,$$
then $x_2^{k+1}$ minimizes the same augmented residual with $x_1^{k+1}$,
$x_2$ variable and $x_3^k$ fixed; then $x_3^{k+1}$ minimizes it with the
first two new blocks; finally
$$u^{k+1}=u^k+A_1x_1^{k+1}+A_2x_2^{k+1}+A_3x_3^{k+1}-b.$$
Only exact attained block minimizers advance the state. A finite solver must
return an explicit failed or cap-exhausted status if it cannot certify a
minimizer. This is a definition of a procedure and asserts no convergence.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Three sequential exact attained minimizers and a dual residual update define the sweep; finite failed or exhausted solvers cannot advance an uncertified state.

2.1 An exact update requires each argmin to be nonempty and attained. The definition requires explicit failure rather than an uncertified approximate point when a finite cap is exhausted, and makes no claim that the cap succeeds or that the outer sequence converges. [A1, F1, given] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, let
$K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be linear,
let $c\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\rho>0$. The primal problem is
$$\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to }Kx+Lz=c,$$
and its Lagrangian is
$\mathcal L((x,z),y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle$.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and the Euclidean space $E=\mathbb R^n$ with inner
product and norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A **relation** $A$ on
$E$ is a subset of $E\times E$; write $a\in A(x)$ exactly when
$(x,a)\in A$. Its graph is this subset. The relation is **monotone** if
$$\langle x-x',a-a'\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for all }(x,a),(x',a')\in A.$$

$E\times E$ is monotone. This definition is finite-dimensional and makes no
claim about infinite-dimensional spaces.

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, let
$K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be linear,
let $c\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\rho>0$. The primal problem is
$$\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to }Kx+Lz=c,$$
and its Lagrangian is
$\mathcal L((x,z),y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle$.
A saddle point means a saddle pair in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]].

For an exact outer sweep with scaled dual $u^k$, compute, in order,
$$x^{k+1}\in\arg\min_x\left(f(x)+\frac\rho2\|Kx+Lz^k-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
$$z^{k+1}\in\arg\min_z\left(g(z)+\frac\rho2\|Kx^{k+1}+Lz-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
then set $r^{k+1}=Kx^{k+1}+Lz^{k+1}-c$ and
$u^{k+1}=u^k+r^{k+1}$. Report also the unscaled dual
$y^k=\rho u^k$, objective $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$, and primal residual $r^k$.
If an exact subproblem has multiple minimizers, choose the unique minimum-norm
member of its nonempty closed convex minimizer set; existence and uniqueness of
that tie-break follow from [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]].

A finite implementation supplies finite inner iteration caps for both solves.
A solve is accepted only with a certificate of an attained global minimizer
before its cap. Return **invalid-input** for invalid dimensions or $\rho\le0$;
return **x-solve-failed**, **x-cap-exhausted**, **z-solve-failed**, or
**z-cap-exhausted** if the corresponding solve fails, is uncertified, or reaches
its cap. A failed sweep does not change the outer state, even if its first
subproblem was solved. These statuses give no approximate convergence guarantee.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Each exact attained block solution uses the unique minimum-norm minimizer tie-break; a failed finite second solve does not commit even a successfully computed first block.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For either block write its subproblem objective as $F(v)+Q(v)$, where $F$ is $f$ or $g$ and $Q$ is the finite continuous convex residual quadratic from [F2]. Its epigraph is the inverse image of the closed set $\operatorname{epi}F$ under the continuous map $(v,s)\mapsto(v,s-Q(v))$, so it is closed by [F1]. If its minimum is attained, the minimum value $a$ is finite: properness gives a finite competitor and neither summand takes $-\infty$. Its minimizer set is nonempty and equals $\{v:F(v)+Q(v)\le a\}$, the inverse image of that closed epigraph under $v\mapsto(v,a)$, hence is closed. The sum of the two convex functions is convex; at two minimizers, convexity bounds every segment value by $a$, while minimality bounds it below by $a$. Thus the minimizer set is convex. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For either block, if its dimension is zero then [F4] makes its Euclidean space the singleton $\{0\}$, so the nonempty minimizer set in step 1.1 is that singleton and its minimum-norm member is unique. In positive dimension, [F3] gives a unique point nearest the origin in the nonempty closed convex minimizer set. Thus the specified tie-break exists and is unique in every dimension, so exact outer sweeps are deterministic. A capped solver that does not certify this attained minimizer returns its stated failure status without changing $(x^k,z^k,u^k)$; hence the finite wrapper makes no claim that every cap will succeed. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $A$ be maximal monotone on $E=\mathbb R^n$ and let $\rho>0$. For every
$y\in E$ there is a unique $x\in E$ with $y-x\in\rho A(x)$. Thus the
resolvent from [[def-resolvent-of-a-monotone-relation]] is an everywhere-defined
map and, for all $y,y'\in E$,

2.1 The polynomial $p-a_0p^\#$ has constant term zero and leading coefficient $1-a_0^2\ne0$, so it is $z$ times a degree-$(n-1)$ polynomial. Hence all zeros of $q$ lie strictly inside the disk. [A1, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
For proper closed convex $f_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, linear
$A_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to\mathbb R^p$, data $b\in\mathbb R^p$, penalty
$\rho>0$, and scaled multiplier $u^k$, the **naive sequential three-block
ADMM** sweep is
$$x_1^{k+1}\in\arg\min_{x_1}f_1(x_1)+\frac\rho2\|A_1x_1+A_2x_2^k+A_3x_3^k-b+u^k\|^2,$$
then $x_2^{k+1}$ minimizes the same augmented residual with $x_1^{k+1}$,
$x_2$ variable and $x_3^k$ fixed; then $x_3^{k+1}$ minimizes it with the
first two new blocks; finally
$$u^{k+1}=u^k+A_1x_1^{k+1}+A_2x_2^{k+1}+A_3x_3^{k+1}-b.$$
Only exact attained block minimizers advance the state. A finite solver must
return an explicit failed or cap-exhausted status if it cannot certify a
minimizer. This is a definition of a procedure and asserts no convergence.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Three sequential exact attained minimizers and a dual residual update define the sweep; finite failed or exhausted solvers cannot advance an uncertified state.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Each displayed block objective is the corresponding convex objective plus a nonnegative continuous quadratic in its block variable; the order fixes later blocks at their newest available values. The update is therefore precisely the sequential Gauss–Seidel extension of the two-block recurrence. [A1, F1, F2, given, given]

2.1 An exact update requires each argmin to be nonempty and attained. The definition requires explicit failure rather than an uncertified approximate point when a finite cap is exhausted, and makes no claim that the cap succeeds or that the outer sequence converges. [A1, F1, given] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, let
$K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be linear,
let $c\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\rho>0$. The primal problem is
$$\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to }Kx+Lz=c,$$
and its Lagrangian is
$\mathcal L((x,z),y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle$.
A saddle point means a saddle pair in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]].

For an exact outer sweep with scaled dual $u^k$, compute, in order,
$$x^{k+1}\in\arg\min_x\left(f(x)+\frac\rho2\|Kx+Lz^k-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
$$z^{k+1}\in\arg\min_z\left(g(z)+\frac\rho2\|Kx^{k+1}+Lz-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
then set $r^{k+1}=Kx^{k+1}+Lz^{k+1}-c$ and
$u^{k+1}=u^k+r^{k+1}$. Report also the unscaled dual
$y^k=\rho u^k$, objective $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$, and primal residual $r^k$.
If an exact subproblem has multiple minimizers, choose the unique minimum-norm
member of its nonempty closed convex minimizer set; existence and uniqueness of
that tie-break follow from [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]].

A finite implementation supplies finite inner iteration caps for both solves.
A solve is accepted only with a certificate of an attained global minimizer
before its cap. Return **invalid-input** for invalid dimensions or $\rho\le0$;
return **x-solve-failed**, **x-cap-exhausted**, **z-solve-failed**, or
**z-cap-exhausted** if the corresponding solve fails, is uncertified, or reaches
its cap. A failed sweep does not change the outer state, even if its first
subproblem was solved. These statuses give no approximate convergence guarantee.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Each exact attained block solution uses the unique minimum-norm minimizer tie-break; a failed finite second solve does not commit even a successfully computed first block.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For either block write its subproblem objective as $F(v)+Q(v)$, where $F$ is $f$ or $g$ and $Q$ is the finite continuous convex residual quadratic from [F2]. Its epigraph is the inverse image of the closed set $\operatorname{epi}F$ under the continuous map $(v,s)\mapsto(v,s-Q(v))$, so it is closed by [F1]. If its minimum is attained, the minimum value $a$ is finite: properness gives a finite competitor and neither summand takes $-\infty$. Its minimizer set is nonempty and equals $\{v:F(v)+Q(v)\le a\}$, the inverse image of that closed epigraph under $v\mapsto(v,a)$, hence is closed. The sum of the two convex functions is convex; at two minimizers, convexity bounds every segment value by $a$, while minimality bounds it below by $a$. Thus the minimizer set is convex. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For either block, if its dimension is zero then [F4] makes its Euclidean space the singleton $\{0\}$, so the nonempty minimizer set in step 1.1 is that singleton and its minimum-norm member is unique. In positive dimension, [F3] gives a unique point nearest the origin in the nonempty closed convex minimizer set. Thus the specified tie-break exists and is unique in every dimension, so exact outer sweeps are deterministic. A capped solver that does not certify this attained minimizer returns its stated failure status without changing $(x^k,z^k,u^k)$; hence the finite wrapper makes no claim that every cap will succeed. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is the
extended-real function on the same Euclidean space
$$f^*(s):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}.$$
When $f(x)=+\infty$, the corresponding term is $-\infty$ and does not increase
the supremum. Its effective domain is
$\operatorname{dom}f^*=\{s:f^*(s)<+\infty\}$.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The extended-real conjugate is a supremum over the Euclidean domain, with infinite primal values contributing negative infinity rather than undefined subtraction.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 For every $x$ with finite $f(x)$, the expression $\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)$ is real; for $f(x)=+\infty$ it contributes $-\infty$ under the stated convention. Thus the supremum is unambiguously defined in $[-\infty,+\infty]$. [A1, given, F1, F2, given]

2.1 If $f$ is proper, choose one $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f$. The finite term $\langle s,x_0\rangle-f(x_0)$ shows $f^*(s)>-\infty$ for every $s$; it may still be $+\infty$. This definition alone does not assert finiteness everywhere. [A1, F1, step 1.1, choose] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
For a relation $A\subseteq E\times E$ and $\rho>0$, define its resolvent as
the inverse relation
$$J_{\rho A}:=(I+\rho A)^{-1},\qquad J_{\rho A}(y)=\{x\in E:y-x\in\rho A(x)\},$$
where $\rho A(x)=\{\rho a:a\in A(x)\}$. Its domain is the set of $y$ for
which this value set is nonempty. At this point it may be partial and
set-valued; full domain and single-valuedness are separate conclusions of
[[thm-maximal-monotone-resolvent-is-firmly-nonexpansive]].
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: The inverse relation at positive rho is allowed to be partial or set-valued until maximal monotonicity supplies the separate full-domain uniqueness theorem.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 The equation $y-x\in\rho A(x)$ means that some $a\in A(x)$ satisfies $y=x+\rho a$; this is precisely the inverse graph of $I+\rho A$. [A1, given, F1, given]
2.1 The value $J_{\rho A}(y)$ is a set and may be empty until a theorem proves existence; the definition itself asserts no surjectivity or uniqueness. [A1, given, F1, given] ∎

conjugate $f^*$ from [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]]
is also proper, closed and convex. The affine-minorant result cited below is
used only to prove properness; closedness and convexity follow directly from
the supremum formula.

selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Choose $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f$ by [F3]. [A1, F1, F4, algebra]

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex. For every
$x,s\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)+f^*(s)\ge\langle s,x\rangle,$$
with extended-real interpretation. Equality holds exactly when
$x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, $f^*(s)<+\infty$, and
$s\in\partial f(x)$; equivalently, for proper convex $f$, equality itself
forces the two finiteness conditions and the subgradient membership.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Fenchel–Young equality forces both finite function values and the stated subgradient membership, whereas the inequality itself uses the extended-real convention.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 If $f(x)=+\infty$, the left side is $+\infty$ because [F1] and properness ensure $f^*(s)>-\infty$, so the inequality is true and equality is impossible. If $f(x)<+\infty$, the term $z=x$ in [F1] gives $f^*(s)\ge\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)$, proving the inequality; if $f^*(s)=+\infty$, equality is again impossible. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 Assume now $f(x)$ and $f^*(s)$ are finite. Equality in step 1.1 holds iff the supremum in [F1] equals its $z=x$ term, which is equivalent to $$\langle s,z\rangle-f(z)\le\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\quad\text{for every }z\in\operatorname{dom}f.$$ Rearranging gives precisely the inequalities in [F2]; for $z\notin\operatorname{dom}f$ they hold automatically. Thus equality is equivalent to $s\in\partial f(x)$, and the converse follows by reversing these inequalities. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_evidence.full_current_interface:
Let $A$ be maximal monotone on $E=\mathbb R^n$ and let $\rho>0$. For every
$y\in E$ there is a unique $x\in E$ with $y-x\in\rho A(x)$. Thus the
resolvent from [[def-resolvent-of-a-monotone-relation]] is an everywhere-defined
map and, for all $y,y'\in E$,
$$\|J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y'\|_2^2\le \langle J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y',y-y'\rangle.$$
This is firm nonexpansiveness; it also implies the map is 1-Lipschitz.
source_evidence.item_specific_mathematical_focus: Maximality and one-point extension give a unique resolvent at every Euclidean input, and monotonicity gives its firm norm inequality.
selected_current_proof_blocks: 1.1 Transform every graph pair $(x,a)\in A$ into $p=x+\rho a$ and $q=x-\rho a$. If two graph pairs are used, then $$\|q-q'\|_2^2\le\|p-p'\|_2^2,$$ because the difference of the right and left sides is $4\rho\langle x-x',a-a'\rangle\ge0$ by [F1]. Also, if $p=p'$, this inequality forces $q=q'$. Thus the rule $T(p)=q$ is a well-defined 1-Lipschitz map on its range $D=\{x+\rho a:(x,a)\in A\}$. [A1, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Fix arbitrary $y\in E$. By [F3], extend $T$ at $y$ by some $q$ satisfying $\|q-(x-\rho a)\|_2\le\|y-(x+\rho a)\|_2$ for every $(x,a)\in A$. Set $\tilde x=(y+q)/2$ and $\tilde a=(y-q)/(2\rho)$. Expanding the squared inequality shows $\langle\tilde x-x,\tilde a-a\rangle\ge0$ for every graph pair, so adjoining $(\tilde x,\tilde a)$ preserves monotonicity. By maximality in [F1], it already belongs to $A$. Hence $y=\tilde x+\rho\tilde a$, proving existence. This also covers an initially empty graph: [F3] gives the extension and maximality rules out the empty graph. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

define for $k\ge0$
$$p_k=J_{\rho B}(w_k),\qquad q_k=J_{\rho A}(2p_k-w_k),\qquad w_{k+1}=w_k+q_k-p_k.$$

specifies exact real arithmetic; a finite implementation that cannot evaluate
a resolvent must report failure and must not advance the exact recurrence. No
termination or convergence claim is part of this algorithm definition.
